[150 F.4th 100]
UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE SECOND CIRCUIT

Tamer S. WASSILY, Petitioner,
v.
Pamela BONDI, United States Attorney
General, Respondent.
Byron E. Velasquez Arreaga, Petitioner,
v.
Pamela Bondi, United States Attorney
General, Respondent.
Docket No. 22-6247
August Term 2023
Docket No. 23-6289
Argued: May 22, 2024
Decided: August 7, 2025
Before:  Wesley, Park, and Robinson, Circuit
Judges.
Judge Robinson dissents in a separate opinion.
Wesley, Circuit Judge:
A noncitizen claiming persecution in his or her
country of nationality may seek asylum in the United
States, either by affirmatively applying for asylum or
by raising a claim for asylum in removal proceedings.
If granted asylum, a noncit izen is protected from
removal and authorized to work in the United States
and to travel abroad.  See 8 U.S.C. § 1158(c)(1).  The
spouse or children of an applicant for asylum may also
be granted asylum status and accompany or follow to

2a

join the original applicant in the United States.  See
id. § 1158(b)(3).
Beyond these benefits, a grant of asylum also
opens a path to citizenship.  Under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b),
a noncitizen who “has been physically present in the
United States for at least one year after being granted
asylum” may apply for lawful permanent resident
status.  Id. § 1159(b).  Assuming other conditions are
met, 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b) provides that the Secretary of
Homeland Security or the Attorney General “may
adjust to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for
permanent residence the status of any alien granted
asylum.”  Id.  Once granted lawful permanent
resident status, a noncitizen may ultimately apply for
citizenship through naturalization.  See generally id.
§ 1427.
These petitions for review, argued in tandem, ask
whether noncitizens seeking adjustment to lawful
permanent resident status under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b)
must maintain their current asylum status or
whether noncitizens may adjust even if their asylum
status has been terminated.  More specifically, they
ask whether a noncitizen seeking adjustment under 8
U.S.C. § 1159(b) must currently be “granted asylum”
to adjust to lawful permanent resident status, or
whether it is enough that a noncitizen was “granted
asylum” at some point in the past, notwithstanding
subsequent termination of that grant of asylum.
Adopting the former reading, the Board of
Immigration Appeals (“BIA”) concluded that
petitioners Tamer Wassily and Byron Velasquez
Arreaga could not adjust to lawful permanent
resident status because their asylum status had been
terminated.  We agree that the plain text of 8 U.S.C.
§ 1159(b) allows only noncitizens with current asylum

3a

status to adjust to lawful permanent resident status
and therefore deny the petitions for review.
BACKGROUND
I.  Tamer Wassily
Tamer Wassily, a native and citizen of Egypt,
entered the United States on a visitor visa in 1993.
He overstayed his visa and was placed in removal
proceedings.  Wassily then applied for asylum,
claiming persecution in Egypt for his Coptic Christian
beliefs; Wassily was granted asylum in 2000.
In 2004, Wassily was convicted of third-degree
stalking, in violation of New York Penal Law
§ 120.50, and child endangerment, in violation of New
York Penal Law § 260.10.  Because of those
convictions, the Department of Homeland Security
(“DHS”) moved to reopen Wassily’s removal
proceedings in order to terminate his asylum status.
The Immigration Judge (“IJ”) granted the motion and
terminated Wassily’s asylum status, finding that
Wassily’s conviction for th ird-degree stalking was a
“particularly serious crime.” 1  The IJ subsequently
denied Wassily’s renewed application for asylum, as
well as his application for withholding of removal and
relief under the Convention Against Torture (“CAT”);
the IJ ordered Wassily removed to Egypt.
Wassily appealed to the BIA; he also moved to
remand, arguing that his co unsel before the IJ was
ineffective by failing to request Wassily’s adjustment

4a

to lawful permanent resident status prior to the
termination of his asylum status. 2  After the BIA
rejected his ineffective assistance of counsel claim and
dismissed his appeal, Wassily filed a petition for
review in this Court.  We granted Wassily’s petition

On remand, the IJ again determined that
Wassily’s third-degree stalking conviction was a
particularly serious crime, therefore terminating
Wassily’s asylum status and rendering him ineligible
for withholding of removal.  Despite terminating
Wassily’s asylum status, the IJ found that Wassily
was eligible to adjust to lawful permanent resident
status under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b) because “[t]he
[Immigration and Nationality Act] does not contain

adjustment of status under [8 U.S.C. § 1159(b)] have
continued asylee status to be eligible for adjustment.”
Wassily v. Bondi, No. 22-6247, Certified Admin. R. at

DHS appealed that decision to the BIA.  While
that appeal was pending, the BIA decided Matter of
T-C-A-, 28 I. & N. Dec. 472 (B.I.A. 2022).  In Matter of
T-C-A-, the BIA concluded that only a noncitizen with
current asylum status can adjust to lawful permanent
resident status under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).  See 28 I. &
N. Dec. at 479.  In other words, the BIA held that “an

II. Byron Velasquez Arreaga
Byron Velasquez Arreaga, a native and citizen of
Guatemala, entered the United States in 1995. The
following year, he was granted asylum.
Velasquez Arreaga then was convicted of multiple
criminal offenses, including, as relevant here, a 2015
conviction for driving while intoxicated, see N.Y. Veh.
& Traf. Law § 1192(2) & (3), and a 2018 conviction for
aggravated driving while intoxicated, see id. § 1192(2-

Citizenship and Immigration Services (“USCIS”)
notified Velasquez Arreaga that it intended to
terminate his asylum status because the 2018
conviction was a particularly serious crime.  DHS
then commenced removal proceedings, charging that
Velasquez Arreaga was removable as a nonimmigrant
who had remained in the United States for longer
than permitted.  See 8 U.S.C. § 1227(a)(1)(B).
Velasquez Arreaga contested that charge, and DHS
then lodged a superseding charge, contending that
Velasquez Arreaga was removable because he did not
possess a valid entry document at the time of
application for admission.  See id. § 1182(a)(7)(A)(i)(I).
The IJ concluded that Velasquez Arreaga’s 2015
and 2018 convictions were particularly serious
crimes, both individually and together, and

citation omitted)).

After an unsuccessful appeal to the BIA,

DISCUSSION
We review the BIA’s determinations of law de
novo.  See Nwozuzu v. Holder , 726 F.3d 323, 326 (2d
Cir. 2013). In a case involving an agency’s
interpretation of a statute, we use the “traditional
tools of statutory constructi on” to “resolve statutory
ambiguities” and “determine the best reading of the
statute.”  Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S.
369, 400–01, 144 S.Ct. 2244, 219 L.Ed.2d 832 (2024).7
I.  Statutory Framework
Asylum is a category of discretionary relief
available to a noncitizen who qualifies as a “refugee”
under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A).  See 8 U.S.C.
§ 1158(b)(1)(A).  As relevant here, a “refugee” under 8
U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is a “person who is outside any

of T-C-A- in rejecting Velasquez Arreaga’s application for
adjustment of status.

Once “granted asylum,” a noncitizen may apply to

II.  “Granted Asylum” Means Current Asylum
Status
These petitions for review turn on the meaning of
“the status of any alien granted asylum”—in
particular, the word “granted.”  Wassily and
Velasquez Arreaga maintain that “granted” should be
read as a past-tense verb.  That is, they argue that
any noncitizen who has ever been “granted” asylum is
eligible to adjust to lawful permanent resident status,
even if the noncitizen’s asylum status was
subsequently terminated.  The Government reads
“granted” as describing a present condition, such that
a noncitizen must currently be “granted asylum” to be
eligible to adjust to lawful permanent resident status
under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).
In our view, 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b) allows only
noncitizens with current asyl um status to adjust to
lawful permanent resident status. 10 A s  w i t h  a n y
question of statutory interpretation, we start with the
text.  See Bartenwerfer v. Buckley, 598 U.S. 69, 74, 143
S.Ct. 665, 214 L.Ed.2d 434 (2023).
Section 1159(b) refers to “the status of an alien
lawfully admitted for permanent residence” and “the

10  Because we independently conclude that 8 U.S.C.
§ 1159(b) precludes a noncitizen with terminated asylum status
from adjusting to lawful perman ent resident status, we reject
Wassily’s argument that the BIA impermissibly applied Matter

F.4th 108, 111 (2d Cir. 2021) (“[J]udicial holdings interpret
existing law and thus operate retroactively.”).

12a

status of any alien gran ted asylum.”  8 U.S.C.
§ 1159(b).  We agree with  the Fourth Circuit’s
observation in Cela  that “the ordinary meaning of
‘status’ signals a present condition,” 75 F.4th at 364—
in particular, a legal condition. 11  It would be odd to
say that someone maintains the present legal
condition of having once been granted asylum at some
point in the past, even though that grant of asylum
was later terminated.  The more natural reading of
“the status of any alien granted asylum” is that a
noncitizen must presently be granted asylum to
adjust to lawful permanen t resident status under 8
U.S.C. § 1159(b).
In fact, if Congress intended to permit anyone
previously granted asylum to become a lawful
permanent resident, as the dissent suggests, there
would be no need for Congress to use the word
“status” at all.  And we reject statutory constructions
that would render a word “insignificant, if not wholly
superfluous.”  Duncan v. Walker , 533 U.S. 167, 174,
121 S.Ct. 2120, 150 L.Ed.2d 251 (2001).

11  See, e.g. , Status, Webster’s Third New International
Dictionary (1981) (“[T]he conditio n (as arising out of age, sex,
mental incapacity, crime, alienage, or public station) of a person
that determines the nature of his legal personality, his legal
capacities, and the nature of the legal relations to the state or to
other persons into which he may enter.”); Status, Black’s Law
Dictionary (5th ed. 1979) (“The legal relation of [an] individual
to [the] rest of the community.”); Status, Oxford English

meaning_and_use#20924305 (last visited Aug. 6, 2025) (“The

movement or action, citizenship, the age of majority, etc.”).

13a

Any lingering uncertainty about the meaning of
“granted” in 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b) is settled by
considering “nearby statutory provisions.”  See
Unicolors, Inc. v. H& M Hennes & Mauritz, L.P. , 595
U.S. 178, 185, 142 S.Ct. 941, 211 L.Ed.2d 586 (2022).
A closer—or even a cursory—look at the neighboring
provision of 8 U.S.C. § 1158(c) confirms our reading of
8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).  As noted above, 8 U.S.C. § 1158(c)
provides that “an alien granted asylum under [8
U.S.C. § 1158(b)]” is pr otected from removal and
permitted to work in the United States and travel
abroad.  See 8 U.S.C. § 1158(c)(1).   But that section
further provides that “[a]sylum granted under [8
U.S.C. § 1158(b)] . . . may be terminated,” and that
can then lead to the noncitizen’s removal.  Id.
§ 1158(c)(2)–(3).
Section 1158(c) consistently uses “granted” to refer
to then-existing asylum status: first, to describe the
benefits available to “an alien granted asylum,” and
second, to refer to the consequences of terminating
that “[a]sylum granted.” 12  Read in that context,
section 1159(b)’s reference to “the status of any alien
granted asylum” is best understood as simply
extending another benefit to a noncitizen with
current asylum status: the opportunity to adjust to
lawful permanent resident status. 13  That reading

such alien.”); id. § 1158(b)(3)(B) (“An unmarried alien who seeks
to accompany, or follow to join, a parent granted asylum under

14a

also best reflects “the statutory scheme as a whole,”
see Soliman v. Subway Franchisee Advert. Fund Tr.,
LTD., 101 F.4th 176, 181 (2d Cir. 2024)—namely, a
statutory framework that  contemplates that a
noncitizen claiming persecution in his or her country
of nationality may first obtain a grant of asylum, then
adjust to lawful permanent resident status, and
ultimately apply for citizenship.
Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga nevertheless
maintain that 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b) cannot require
current asylum status because other, differently
worded provisions in 8 U.S.C. § 1159 require a
noncitizen to meet some other “present” qualification.
The dissent likewise maintains that 8 U.S.C. § 1159
“expressly includes continuing status requirements
where applicable[ ] and [ ] does not apply one to
individuals ‘granted asylum.’ ”  Dissenting Op. at
109–10.
Besides assuming its conclusion—that the phrase
“granted asylum” does not impose a continuing status
requirement—the dissent’s argument cannot
overcome the clear meaning of the statutory text.
True, other parts of 8 U.S.C. § 1159 use varying
language to require that a noncitizen seeking
adjustment to lawful permanent resident status
maintain some other current condition. 14  Those

B. Respondent is not eligible for asylum
pursuant to INA § 208 because his conviction
for NYPL § 120.50(3) is a particularly serious
crime.
An applicant is not eligible for asylum if he has
been convicted, by a final judgment, of a particularly
serious crime.  INA § 208(b)(2)(A).  “The Attorney
General (or his agents) may determine that a crime is
particularly serious for purposes of the asylum
statute . . . even though it is not an aggravated
felony.”  Nethagani v. Mukasey, 532 F.3d 150, 156 (2d
Cir. 2008); see also INA § 208(b)(2)(B)(ii).  If the
Immigration Judge determines that an applicant has
been convicted of a partic ularly serious crime, the
applicant necessarily constitutes a danger to the
community, Flores v. Hold er, 779 F.3d 159, 167 (2d
Cir. 2015) (citing Nethagan i, 522 F.3d at 154 n.l).
Therefore, the proper focus for determining whether

47a

a crime is particularly serious is on the nature of the
crime and not the likelihood of future serious
misconduct.  Matter of N-A-M-, 24 I&N Dec. 336, 342
(BIA 2007).
In “determin[ing] whether the crime was
particularly serious” the Immigration Judge should
consider “(1) the nature of the conviction, (2) the
circumstances and underlying facts of the conviction,
(3) the type of sentence imposed, and (4) whether the
type and circumstances of the crime indicate that the
alien will be a danger to the community,” Nethagani,
532 F.3d at 155 (citing Matter of Frentescu, 18 I&N
Dec. 244, 247 (BIA 1982), modi fied, Matter of C-, 20
I&N Dec. 529 (BIA 1992)).  The judge should first
determine whether “the elements of the offense . . .
potentially bring the crime into a category of
particularly serious crimes.”  N-A-M-, 24 I&N Dec. at
342.  If not, “the individual facts and circumstances of
the offense are of no consequence” and the applicant
is not barred from asylum.  N-A-M-, 24 I&N Dec. at
342.
In this case, the elemen ts of the crime, NYPL
§ 120.50(3), do potentially bring the crime into a
category of particularly serious crimes.  Under NYPL
§ 120.50(3), an individual is guilty of stalking in the
third degree when:
[he or she] . . . with in tent to harass, annoy or
alarm a specific person, intentionally engages
in a course of conduct directed at such person
which is likely to cause such person to
reasonably fear physical injury or serious
physical injury, the commission of a sex
offense against, or the kidnapping, unlawful
imprisonment or death of such person or a
member of such person’s immediate family.

NYPL § 120.50(3).  Consider ing that the Second
Circuit has found that crimes against persons are
more likely to be particularly serious than crimes
against property, and that to be convicted, the

among other outcomes, serious injury, a sexual
offense, or death, I find that the elements of this crime
do indeed potentially bring this crime into a category

703,712 (BIA 2016), N-A-M-, 24 I&N Dec. at 343; see

adjustment of status under INA § 209(b) have
continued asylee status to be eligible for adjustment.
See INA § 209(b)(3).  Adjustment of status under INA
§ 209(a) requires a refugee admitted under INA § 207
and applying to adjust their status under INA
§ 209(a) to maintain their status, but the INA
contains no analogous requirement clause for
adjustment of status under INA § 209(b).  See
§ 209(a)(1)(A) (making eligible “[a]ny alien who had
been admitted to the United States under section 207
. . . whose admission has not been terminated. . .”);
INA § 209(b)(l)-(5).  Rather, Respondent need only
continue to meet the definition of a refugee under INA
§ 101(a)(42)(A).  See IN A § 209(b)(3).  Here, I
terminated Respondent’s asylee status because he
was convicted of a particularly serious crime.  See
INA § 208(b)(2)(A).  Respon dent was convicted of
stalking in the third degree in violation of NYPL

53a

§ 120.50(3) and was ordered to serve three years of
probation.  (Ex. B5, Tab D).  I terminated
Respondent’s asylee status because of his conviction
for a particularly serious crime, not because he ceased
to possess a well-founded fear of persecution.
Respondent was previously granted asylum based on
his well-founded fear of persecution should he be
returned to Egypt, and no evidence has been
submitted to suggest that country conditions have
changed so extensively as to eradicate the source of
his fear.
Notably, the most recent U.S. Department of State
Human Rights Report for Egypt (“2018 DOS Report”)
states that terrorist organizations caused arbitrary
and unlawful deprivation of life, by conducting deadly
attacks at places of worship.  (2018 DOS Report at 2).5
Further, the U.S. Department of State’s International
Religious Freedom Report for Egypt (“2018 Religious
Freedom Report”) states in Egypt “Islam is the
religion of the state.”  (2018 Religious Freedom Report
at 1).  The government officially recognizes
Christianity; however, Coptic Christians continued to
suffer violence in Egypt.  Id.  In 2016 and 2017
bombings occurred at Coptic churches in Cairo,
Alexandria, and Tanta, which killed more than eighty
people.  Id.
Further, the Egyptian government has not
effectively prosecuted perpetrators of violence, as
authorities responded to attacks against Christians

5  I take administrative notice of the most recent
Department of State Human Rights Report and International
Religious Freedom Report for Egypt.  See Shao v. Mukasey, 546
F.3d 138, 166-68 (2d Cir. 2008); Yang v. McElroy, 277 F.3d
158,162-63 & n.4 (2d Cir. 2002).

54a

through arbitration sessions rather than prosecution.
Id.  Moreover, “religious freedom and human rights
activists said government officials’ sometimes did not
extend procedural safeguards or rights of due process
to members of minority faiths.”  Id. at 11.  Violent
attacks against Christians continue in Egypt.  This
past year armed assailants attacked three buses
carrying Christian pilgrims to a monastery, killing
seven and wounding nineteen.  Id.  at 2.  Further,
there have been reported incidents of mob action
against, and collective punishment of, Christians.  Id.
at 17.  For instance, Muslim residents in Upper
Egypt, “protested Christian religious services held in
an unlicensed church, and looted four Christian-
owned houses before setting them on fire.  The attack
injured two Coptic villagers.”  Id.
Consequently, I find that Respondent, a Coptic
Christian, continues to meet the definition of a
refugee and satisfies this element of eligibility of
adjustment of status under INA § 209(b).  See
INA§ 101(a)(42)(A).
4. No Firm Resettlement
The fourth requirement of INA § 209(b) is that
Respondent not be firmly resettled in another
country.  Respondent has not resettled in any country
and has maintained his residence in the U.S.
5. Admissible at Examination for Adjustment
of Status
The fifth requirement of INA § 209(b) is that
Respondent be admissible at the time of examination
for adjustment of status.  In  this case, Respondent is
not admissible to the U.S. and thus requires an INA
§ 209(c) waiver to satisfy the final statutory

55a

requirement for adjustment  of status.  See INA
§ 209(b)(5).
An INA § 209(c) waiver is discretionary and may
be granted for “humanitarian purposes, to assure
family unity, or when it is  otherwise in the public
interest.”  Id.  The discretionary analysis of this
waiver requires balancing favorable and unfavorable
factors that may include family ties within the U.S.;
residency of long duration in this country;
employment history; existence of value and service to
the community; proof of genuine rehabilitation of a
criminal record; evidence attesting to a Respondent’s
good or bad character; and the nature and underlying
circumstances of inadmissibility grounds.  See Matter
of C-V-T, 22 I&N Dec. 7,  11 (BIA 1998); Matter of
Marin, 16 I&N Dec. 581, 587 (BIA 1978), abrogated
on other grounds by Matter of Edwards, 20 I&N Dec.
191 (BIA 1990); see also Chan  v. Gantner, 464 F.3d
289, 295 (2d Cir. 2006).
Aliens who have committed violent or dangerous
crimes will not be granted such a waiver unless the
applicant “clearly demonstrates that the denial of
status adjustment would result in exceptional and
extremely unusual hardship.”  Matter of Jean, 23 I&N
Dec. 373, 383 (A.G. 2002).  Depending on the gravity
of the underlying offense, however, a showing of such
hardship may still be insufficient.  Id. at 384.
Although the crime committed by Respondent did not
involve violent conduct, I find that it is a dangerous
offense because it requires that the victim
“reasonably fear physical injury or serious physical
injury” and because the victim in this case was a
minor.  However, I find that Respondent has
established that his removal would result in
exceptional and extremely unusual hardship.  In

56a

making this determination, I have considered the
following factors:  1) Resp ondent’s lengthy residence
in the U.S. which now exceeds twenty-five years;
2) his lack of family ties in Egypt and his substantial
family ties in this country  as well as his reliance on
his family; 3) Respondent’s  adherence to a religious
minority in Egypt which has been and continues to be
subjected to violent attack and severe discrimination,
and 4) Respondent’s intelle ctual disorder which will
likely increase his vulnerability to harm.  See Ex. RB-
9.  Having made a threshold determination that
Respondent has established the requisite level of
hardship, I must determine whether a favorable
exercise of discretion is warranted.
Respondent has established numerous positive
equities.  He submitted evidence that he pays taxes
and a letter of support from his employer, for whom
he has worked for the past nineteen years.  (Ex. RB5,
Tab E, Ex. RB10).  Further, Respondent has lived in
the U.S., with his family, for almost thirty-years.  He
is a Coptic Christian and received asylum in 2000
based on his well-founded fear of persecution in Egypt
on account of his religion.  As noted above,
Respondent’s removal to Egypt would likely cause
him to experience significant hardship as he has no
family there and is a member of a minority religion in
Egypt.
Although an extremely close case, I find that
Respondent’s positive equities outweigh the adverse
factors in the record.  Respondent has a significant
criminal history and has committed a particularly
serious crime.  In 1998, he pled guilty to disorderly
conduct in violation of NYPL § 240.20(7), and in 2004,
he pled guilty to stalking  in the third degree in
violation of NYPL § 120.50(3) and to endangering the

57a

welfare of a child in viol ation of NYPL § 260.10(1).
(Ex. RB5, Tab D).  Respondent’s testimony suggests
that he fails to take respon sibility for his actions, or
indeed acknowledge any wrongdoing on his part.
While I found Respondent competent to provide
testimony, I recognize that his intellectual disorder
may play a role in his failure to express remorse.  Id.
With regard to rehabilitation, however, Respondent
has not reoffended since 2004.  A lengthy period
during which an alien has not reoffended is a
significant indicator of rehabilitation.
I find that humanitarian considerations weigh in
favor of a discretionary grant.  Respondent still
qualifies as a refugee as he has a well-founded fear of
persecution in Egypt on account of his religion.
Further, all of Respondent’s family reside in the U.S.
and family unification is a significant positive factor
in this case.  In this case , by a narrow margin, I find
that the favorable discretionary factors in this record
outweigh the adverse factors.  However, I caution
Respondent that any future criminal conduct will
likely result in his removal from the United States.
Accordingly, I grant Respondent’s application for a
waiver under INA § 209(c).
After a careful review of the record, the following
Orders are entered:
ORDERS
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that Respondent’s
asylee status be TERMINATED;
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that Respondent’s
applications for asylum under INA § 208(a) and
withholding of removal under INA § 241(b)(3), be
DENIED;

58a

IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that Respondent’s
application for an INA § 209(c) Waiver be
GRANTED; and
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that Respondent’s
application for adjustment  of status under INA
§209(b) be GRANTED.

The respondent, a native and citizen of Egypt,
appeals from an Immigration Judge’s decision dated
September 3, 2008, denying his application for
asylum and withholding of removal under sections
208 and 241(b)(3) of the Immigration and Nationality
Act (“Act”), 8 U.S.C. §§ 1158 and 1231(b)(3), and for
protection under the Convention Against  Torture
(“CAT”), 8 C.F.R. §§ 1208.16-1208.18.  While the
respondent’s appeal was pending, he filed a motion to
remand the proceedings to the Immigration Court
under Matter of Compean 24 I&N Dec. 710 (A.G.
2009), based on his prio r counsel’s deficient

63a

performance and so that he may apply for adjustment
of status.  The motion to remand will be denied, and
the appeal will be dismissed.
We review the findings of fact, including the
determination of credibility, made by the
Immigration Judge under a “clearly erroneous”
standard.  8 C.F.R. § 1003.1(d)(3)(i); Matter of S-H-,
23 I&N Dec. 462 (BIA 2002).  There is clear error in a
factual finding when the reviewing Board member or
panel is left with the definite and firm conviction that
a mistake has been made.  See Matter of R-S-H-,  23
I&N Dec. 629, 637 (BIA 2003).  We review all other
issues, including whether the parties have met the
relevant burden of proof, and issues of discretion,
under a de novo standard.  8 C.F.R. § 1003.1(d)(3)(ii);
Matter of A-S-B-, 24 I&N Dec. 493 (BIA 2008).
Since the respondent’s asylum application was
filed after May 11, 2005, it is governed by the
provisions of the REAL ID Act. 1  See Matter of S-B-,
24 I&N Dec. 42 (BIA 2006).  Hence, the amendments
made by the REAL ID Act to section 208(b)(1)(B) of
the Act apply to this case.
The respondent’s deficient performance of counsel
claim, based on his former counsel’s failure to request
that the respondent be allowed to pursue adjustment
of status prior to termin ation of his asylee status
consistent with Matter of K-A-, 23 I&N Dec. 661 (BIA
2004), does not warrant reopening of these
proceedings.  We note that the Attorney General
vacated the decision cited by the respondent in his
motion to remand.  Matter of Compean, Bangaly &
J-E-C-, 25 I&N Dec. 1 (A.G. 2009), vacating 24 I&N

1  See I.J. at 15.

64a

Dec. 710 (A.G. 2009).  Pending rulemaking
procedures, the Board was directed to “apply the pre-
Compean standards to all pending and future motions
to reopen based upon ineffective assistance of counsel,
regardless of when such  motions were filed.”
Accordingly, we apply the standards articulated in
Matter of Lozada, 19 I&N Dec. 637 (BIA 1988).  The
respondent fails to meet hi s burden of establishing
that subject counsel’s alleged failings were
“egregious?”  Changxu Jiang v. Mukasey,  522 F.3d
266, 270 (2d Cir. 2008) (“[t]he BIA properly
determined that Jiang did not make a showing of
ineffective assistance of counsel because he did not
establish that his prior counsel’s handling of the case
was so egregious that his hearing was rendered
unfair”).  The respondent has failed to demonstrate
that competent counsel would have acted otherwise,
and that he was prejudiced by his prior counsel’s
performance.  See Romano v. INS, 399 F.3d 109, 112
(2d Cir. 2005).  Further, the Second Circuit has held
that an attorney’s “strategic decisions” in asylum
proceedings cannot be the basis for an ineffective
assistance claim.  Changxu Jiang v. Mukasey, supra,
at 270.  Lastly, on the eviden ce before us, it does not
appear that the respondent would be prima facie
eligible for adjustment of status.
An alien convicted of a “particularly serious crime”
is ineligible for withholding of removal under either
section 241(b)(3) of the Act or the CAT.  See section
241(b)(3)(B)(ii) of the Act; 8 C.F.R. § 1208.16(d)(2).
However, deferral of removal under the CAT remains
available to such an alien.  8 C.F.R. § 1208.17(a).
Whether a criminal offense qualifies as a
particularly serious crime is a question of law that we
review de novo, 8 C.F.R. § 1003.1(d)(3)(ii).  As the

65a

respondent was not sentenced to a term of
imprisonment of at least 5 years, the offense does not
automatically qualify as a particularly serious crime.
Accordingly, we look first to the statutory elements of
his crime to determine whether it was particularly
serious.  Matter of N-A-M-, 24 I&N Dec. 336, 342 (BIA
2007).  If an offense qualifies as a particularly serious
crime based solely on its elements, then no further
inquiry is required and the application for
withholding of removal must be pretermitted.  Id. at
342-43.  Conversely, if the offense elements clearly do
not define a particularly serious crime, then the
section 241 (b)(3)(B)(ii) preclusion is inapplicable and
no further inquiry into the factual circumstances of
the crime is permitted.  Id. at 342.  However, there
are situations where examination of the offense
elements will establish only that the offense is
potentially a particularly serious crime, id at 342; that
is, that some offenses in violation of the statute are
particularly serious crimes while others may not be.
Once the elements of the offense are examined and
found to potentially bring the offense within the
ambit of a particularly serious crime, the burden is on
the applicant to come forward with evidence to
establish mitigating facts that would preclude such a
designation in the particular case.  See 8 C.F.R.
§§ 1208.16(d)(2) and 1240.8(d) (indicating that where
a ground for mandatory denial of an application for
relief may apply, the applicant bears the burden of
proving by a preponderance of the evidence that the
ground is inapplicable).  In seeking to meet this
burden, the respondent may adduce any reliable
information, including conviction records and
sentencing information, as well as other information
outside the confines of a record of conviction.  Matter

66a

of N-A-M-, supra.  However, factors that are
subsequent and unrelated to the commission of the
offense, such as rehabilitation, bear only on
sentencing and are irrelevant to a determination of
whether a crime is “particularly serious?”  Matter of
N-A-M-, supra, at 343 (citing Matter of Y-L-, A-G-, &
R-S-R-, 23 I&N Dec. 270, 273-74, 277-78 (A.G. 2002)).
We affirm the Immigration Judge’s determination
that the respondent’s ‘‘conviction for stalking in the
third degree under NYPL section 120.50(3)
constitutes a particularly serious crime.”  See I.J. at
16.  The Immigration Judge properly considered
details contained in the pre-sentencing report in
making the finding that:
The repugnant and terrifying nature of the
threats against the victim are further
aggravated by the fact that the victim was
sixteen years old and the fact that, by [the]
[r]espondent’s own admission, he was often
intoxicated during the commission of this
crime.
See I.J. at 17, As the respondent has been convicted of
a particularly serious crime, he is therefore ineligible
for asylum and withholding of removal under the Act,
as well as, withholding of removal under the CAT.
See section 241(b)(3)(B)(ii) of the Act; 8 C.F.R.
§ 1208.16(d)(2).
To qualify for deferral of removal under the CAT,
an applicant must demonstrate that it is more likely
than not that he will suffer “torture” in Egypt.  For an
act to constitute “torture” within the meaning of the
CAT it must be:
(1) an act causing severe physical or mental
pain or suffering; (2) intentionally inflicted;

67a

(3) for a proscribed purpose; (4) by or at the
instigation of or with the consent or
acquiescence of a public official who has
custody or physical control of the victim; and
(5) not arising from lawful sanctions.
Matter of J-E-, 23 I&N Dec. 291, 297 (BIA 2002); see
also 8 C.F.R. § 1208.18(a).  The Immigration Judge
denied the respondent’s application for deferral of
removal under the CAT after finding that the
respondent failed to carry hi s burden of proof (I.J. at
18-21).  See 8 C.F.R. § 1208.17.  We adopt and affirm
the Immigration Judge’s decision for the reasons
stated therein.  Given the record before the
Immigration Judge, we conclude that there is no error
in his denial of protection.  In this regard, the
respondent’s claim is based on a claim of assumptions
and speculation ( e.g., that the authorities in Egypt
will have an interest in him based on his activities in
this country, that they will become aware of his
return to Egypt, that they will subject him to
treatment amounting to torture, that the Egyptian
government will not protect him).  See 8 C.F.R.
§ 1208.18 (“Torture is an ex treme form of cruel and
inhuman treatment. . . .”); Matter of J-F-F-, 23 I&N
Dec, 912 (A.G. 2006) (eligibility for deferral of removal
under Convention Against Torture cannot be
established by stringing together a series of
suppositions where the evidence does not establish
that each step in the hypothetical chain of events is
more likely than not to happen); Matter of M-B-A-, 23
I&N Dec. 474, 479-80 (BIA 2002).
The respondent has failed to establish how the
Egyptian authorities would have knowledge of any of
the following: (1) that he is a former asylee; (2) his
activities in the United States; or (3) that he has

68a

damaged Egypt’s reputation abroad.  The respondent
has therefore failed to establish that it is more likely
than not that he will be subjected to torture at the
hands of the Egyptian authorities.  The respondent
has also failed to establish that it would not be
reasonable for him to relocate within Egypt.  See 8
C.F.R. § 1208.16(b)(3)(l).   The respondent’s
arguments regarding the li kelihood of torture are
speculative and not based on evidence in the record.
See Matter of J-F-F-, supra, at 917 (applicant fails to
carry burden of proof if ev idence is speculative or
inconclusive).
Accordingly, the following orders shall be entered.
ORDER:  The motion to remand is denied.
FURTHER ORDER:  The respondent’s appeal is
dismissed.

A. Legal Standards
I. Credibility
Before determining whether the Respondent
meets the statutory criteria required for withholding
of removal and CAT relief, I must address the
credibility of his testimony in its entirety.  Matter of
O–D–, 21 I. & N. Dec.  1079, 1081 (BIA 1998).  The
applicant’s own testimony will suffice to carry his
burden of proof, provided  that such testimony is
believable, consistent, and sufficiently detailed to
provide a plausible and coherent account of the basis
of his fear.  Matter of Dass, 20 I. & N. Dec. 120, 124
(BIA 1989); 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13( a).  Furthermore, the
applicant may be given the “benefit of the doubt” if
there is some ambiguity regarding an aspect of his
asylum claim.  Matter of Y–B–, 21 I. & N. Dec. 1136,
1139 (BIA 1998).  Additionally, the applicant may be
found credible even if he cannot recall specific facts.
See, e.g., Matter of B–, 21 I. & N. Dec. 66, 70-71 (BIA
1995) (explaining aliens who fled persecution may
have difficulty remembering exact dates when
testifying, and such failure to provide precise dates
may not indicate deception).

92a

The REAL ID Act of 2005 2 amended various
sections of the INA to the adjudication of asylum,
withholding of removal, and CAT applications.  Pub.
L. No. 109–13, Div. B, 119 Stat. 231 (2005).  I have
not applied these provisions in this matter because
respondent’s initial application for asylum was filed
prior to the date of enactment of the REAL ID Act.
ii. Asylum
(a) Statutory Eligibility
In order to demonstrate statutory eligibility for
relief, an applicant is requir ed to prove that he is a
“refugee.”  INA § 208(b)(1).  In order for the applicant
to prove his “refugee” status, he must demonstrate
that he falls within the scope of the following:
[P]erson who is outside any country of such
person’s nationality . . . and is unable or
unwilling to return to, and is unable and
unwilling to avail himself or herself to the
protection of that country because of
persecution or a well-founded fear of
persecution on account of race, religion,
nationality, membership in a particular social
group, or political opinion.
INA § 101(a)(42)(A).
If an applicant establishes that he has suffered
past persecution, his well-founded fear of future
persecution is presumed, unless rebutted by DHS.  8
C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(1)(I).  If an applicant fails to prove
past persecution, he must demonstrate that there is a

(b) Discretion
An applicant who establishes statutory eligibility
for asylum still bears the burden of demonstrating
that he merits a grant of asylum as a matter of
discretion.  INA § 208(b)(1); see also Cardoza-

whether a favorable exercise of discretion is
warranted, both favorable and adverse factors should
be considered.  Matter of Pula, 19 I. & N. Dec. 467,

exercising their of discretion.  Matter of H–, 21 I. & N.

iii. Withholding of Removal Under INA
Section 241(b)(3)
Under INA section 241(b)(3), the applicant bears
the evidentiary burden of proof and persuasion with
respect to withholding of removal.  Matter of Acosta,
19 I. & N. Dec. 211, 214–15 (BIA 1985), modified,
Matter of Mogharrabi, 19 I.  & N. Dec. 439, 446–47
(BIA 1987); 8 C.F.R. §§ 1208.13(a), 1208.16(b) (2004).
To satisfy his burden of proof, the applicant must
demonstrate that, if returned to his country, his life
or freedom would be threatened on account of his race,
religion, nationality, membership in a particular
social group, or political opinion.  INA § 241(b)(3); see

also Zhang v. INS, 386 F.3d 66, 71 (2d Cir. 2004).  To
make this showing, the a pplicant must establish a
“clear probability” of persecution, meaning it is “more

on account of a protected ground if returned to the
country from which he seeks withholding of removal.

Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or

of M–B–A–, 23 I. & N. Dec. 474, 477–78 (BIA 2002).

would involve the intentional infliction of severe pain
or suffering by, or at the instigation of, or with the
consent or acquiescence of a public official.  8 C.F.R.
§ 1208.18(a)(1).

B. Analysis
I. Respondent’s Testimony Was Not Credible
and the Documentary Evidence in the
Record Contradicted His Testimonial
Claims
I find that Respondent’s testimony regarding his
criminal convictions was so dishonest, that it casts
doubt on the veracity of his testimony as a whole.
Respondent testified that he was arrested for the
first time in 1998 because some girls he encountered
on the street incorrectly believed he was attempting
to expose himself.  He further testified that the 1998
arrest did not result in a conviction.  However,
Respondent’s testimony is inconsistent with the
record, which contains a certificate of conviction
indicating that on September 24, 1998, Respondent
was convicted of disorderly conduct in violation of
NYPL section 240.20(7).  [Ex. 5.]  Moreover,
Respondent testified that after the arrest, he
underwent voluntary psychi atric treatment to learn
to control his sexual compulsion.  Yet, his doctor’s
notes reflect he did not discuss his compulsion until
months into treatment, and only did so on his doctor’s
prompting after Respondent’s brother requested a
letter stating that Respondent was undergoing
treatment for his compulsion.  [Ex. 9.]
Similarly, Respondent denies engaging in any
criminal conduct with respect to his 2004 convictions.
He stated that his interactions with Angela were
brief, limited to discussions about movies and music,
and only took place over the telephone or at the mall
where she was employed.  He further testified that he
never made any sexual references or threatened
Angela during their conversations, and that he was

96a

“shocked and surprised’’ about the accusations
against him.  However, during his plea colloquy,
Respondent admitted that he “followed, stared at and
placed in fear for her safety and had sexually explicit
conversations with sixteen-y ear-old girl.”  [Ex. R2,
Attach. A, at 12.]  Asked why he would have admitted
committing those acts if he did not, Respondent stated
that he wanted to get out of jail and that his attorney
advised him to do so, then stated that he did not swear
to not having been promised any benefits in exchange
for his guilty plea.  Yet, th e transcript from his plea
colloquy shows that Respondent did swear to tell the
truth.  [Ex. R2, Attach. A., at 4.]  Presented with this
inconsistency between his testimony and the record,
Respondent changed his testimony and stated instead
that at the time of his plea colloquy, he did not
remember being promised any benefits in exchange
for his guilty plea.  I do not find Respondent’s
explanation of the inconsistencies between his
testimony and his plea colloquy credible, and find
instead that his explanations, which were elicited
upon being confronted with inconsistencies, were
attempts to preserve his credibility.  See Majidi v.
Gonzales, 430 F.3d 77, 80–81 (2d Cir. 2005) (an
applicant’s explanations need not be credited unless
those explanations would compel a reasonable factfinder to do so).
Respondent also testified that he was only
sentenced to probation in connection with his 2004
convictions and that the criminal court did not place
any sex offender conditions on him.  Again, the record
undermines his testimony, as the plea transcript
shows that the court stated that Respondent’s
sentence “include[s] sex offender conditions,” and that
his attorney advised him of the conditions.  [Ex. R2,

97a

Attach. A, at 3-4.]  Furthermore, the record contains
evidence that such sex offender conditions included,
inter alia,  that he remain within the court’s
jurisdiction, that he participate in and successfully
complete a sex offender treatment program, and that
he not be alone with any child under eighteen years
of age.  [Ex. R4, Attach. A.]  Additionally, Respondent
was re-sentenced to and placed under probation for an
additional nine months due to his violation of the
aforementioned sex offender conditions [Ex. R4,
Attach. A.]  Thus, I find it hard to believe that
Respondent was unaware of his sex offender
conditions, and find that he  testified that he was not
placed under any such conditions in an attempt to
minimize his culpability and distance himself from a
“sex offender” label.
Based on the foregoing, I find Respondent’s
testimony not be credible, as it was inconsistent with
the record.  See Matter of S–M–J–, 21 I. & N. Dec. at
729 (testimony is not consider ed credible when it is
inconsistent).
ii. Respondent is Barred from Asylum Due
to His Conviction for a Particularly
Serious Crime
Respondent is subject to a mandatory denial of his
application for asylum because his conviction for
stalking in the third degree under NYPL section
120.50(3) constitutes a particularly serious crime.
See INA § 208(b)(2)(A)(ii).  I recognize that
Respondent’s crime is not an aggravated felony under
INA Section 101(a)(43).  Nevertheless, the Second
Circuit recently held in Nethagani v. Mukasey, 532
F.3d 150, 156 (2d Cir. 2008), that IJs “may determine
that a crime is particularly serious for purposes of the

98a

asylum statute . . . even though it is not an
aggravated felony.”
To determine whether Respondent’s conviction is
for a particularly serious crime, I must use the factors
set forth in Matter of Frentescu, 18 I. & N. Dec. 244
(BIA 1982), superceded by statute on other grounds.
See Nethagani, 532 F.3d at 155 (applying Frentescu
factors).  These factors incl ude; (1) the nature of the
conviction; (2) the circumstances and underlying facts
of the conviction; and (3) the type of sentence imposed.
See Matter of Frentescu, 18 I. & N. Dec. at 247.
Notably I need not determine whether Respondent is
a danger to the community.3  See Matter of N–A–M–,
24 I. & N. Dec. 336, 342 (B IA 2007); see also Matter
of Caballe, 19 I. & N. Dec. 357 (BIA 1996) (“the proper
focus . . . is on the nature of the crime and not the
likelihood of future misconduct).  Furthermore, if “the
elements of the offense ar e examined and found to
potentially bring the offense within the ambit of a
particularly serious crime, all reliable information
may be considered” in making the determination.
Matter of N–A–M–, 24 I. & N. Dec. 336, 342 (BIA
2007).
I find that the elements, or nature of, Respondent’s
statute of conviction bring it within the ambit of a
particularly serious crime because it occurs when:
A person . . . with intent to harass, annoy,
or alarm a specific person, intentionally
engages in a course of conduct directed at such
person which is likely to cause such person to

3  I note, however, that Respondent’s failure to take
responsibility for his actions and his attempts to minimize his
culpability evidence a lack of rehabilitation, and thus, that he
may pose continuing harm to the community.  See Part IV(B)(I).

99a

reasonably fear physical injury, or serious
physical injury, the commission of a sex
offense against, or the kidnapping, unlawful
imprisonment or death of such person or a
member of such person’s immediate family.
NYPL § 120.50(3); see Matter of Frentescu, 18 I. & N.
Dec. at 247; Matter of N–A–M–, 24 I. & N. Dec. at 342.
The statute under which Respondent was convicted is
for a crime against a person.  In this case the effect of
such crime is particularly terrifying and damaging to
the victim, given that she was only sixteen years old.
Therefore, I may look to all reliable information in
assessing the severity of Respondent’s crime,
“including the conviction records and sentencing
information, as well as other information outside the
confines of the record of conviction.”  Matter of
N–A–M–, 24 I. & N. Dec. at 342; see also Matter of
L–S–, 22 I. & N. Dec. 645, 654–56 (BIA 1999) (looking
beyond the elements of the crime and examining the
actual circumstances of the crime).
The pre-sentence report contains disturbing
details of the acts underling Respondent’s convictions.
Respondent stalked the victim for three months and
made numerous calls to her, during which he told her
“he was masturbating and that he wanted to rape
her.”  [Ex. R7, Attach. B, at 3.]  Respondent also
threatened the victim’s life over the course of several
months, and stated that her family should “start
making [her] funeral arrangements.”  [Ex. R7, Attach.
B, at 3.]  He also obta ined “personal information
regarding the victim (such as how many siblings she
had) and used this [information] when telephoning
her” in order to instill further fear in her.  [Ex. R7,
Attach. B, at 3.]  The repugnant and terrifying nature
of the threats against the victim are further

100a

aggravated by the fact th at the victim was sixteen
years old and the fact that, by Respondent’s own
admission, he was often intoxicated during the
commission of this crime.  [Ex. R2, Attach. A, at 8
(admitting to stalking a sixteen-year-old girl); Ex. R7,
Attach. B, at 3 (stating, “I did do what I was charged
with but I was drunk.”)]
Lastly, I recognize that Respondent was not
sentenced to a term of imprisonment, and was only
ordered to serve probation and to comply with several
sex offender conditions.  [Ex. R4, Attach. A; Ex. R7,
Attach. A.]  However, as explained in Matter of
N–A–M–, 22 I. & N. Dec. at 342, “the sentence
imposed is not the most accurate or salient factor
to consider when determining the seriousness of
an offense” because it in volves factors unrelated
to the commission of the offe nse.  Accordingly, as in
N–A–M–, 22 I. & N. Dec. at 343, I find that
Respondent’s offense is particularly serious in spite of
the fact that he was not sentenced to a term of
imprisonment.
In sum, I find that the nature and underlying facts
of Respondent’s conviction render his crime
particularly serious.  Therefore, I find that
Respondent is statutorily  barred from asylum, and
deny his application for such relief.
iii. Respondent is Barred from Withholding
of Removal Under INA section 241(b)(3)
Due to His Conviction for a Particularly
Serious Crime
As explained above, I find that Respondent’s
conviction under NYPL section 120.50(3) constitutes
a particularly serious crime.  See Part IV(B)(ii) supra.
Aliens convicted of particularly serious crimes are

101a

ineligible for withholding of removal under INA
section 241(b)(3).  See INA § 241(b)(3)(B)(ii); see also
Matter of N–A–M–, 24 I. & N. Dec. at 337–38 (“a
particularly serious crime need not be an aggravated
felony”).  Therefore, Respondent’s application for
relief under INA section 241(b)(3) is denied.
iv. Respondent is Barred from Withholding
of Removal Under the CAT Due to His
Conviction for a Particularly Serious
Crime and Failed to Carry His Burden of
Proof With Respect to Deferral of
Removal
Respondent claims that considering the following
factors in the aggregate, he will more likely than not
be tortured in Egypt: becaus e he is required to carry
an identity document in Egypt, government officials
will learn of and punish him for his past problems
with Muslims; due to his request for asylum and
conviction for a sexual offense in the United States,
he could be convicted under Egyptian law section
80(d), for damaging Egypt’s reputation abroad; as a
Copt, he is more likely to suffer police abuse than non-
Copts; and because he has resided in the United
States for fifteen years and is a Christian, he will be
considered an ally of the enemy Christian West,
which is viewed as responsible for the war in Iraq and
for attacking Arab Muslims.  [Ex. 2, Attachs. A–C; Ex.
R5; R11, Attachs. A–B; Ex. RI3.]  Having considered
the documentary and testimonial evidence, I will now
assess whether Respondent has met his burden of
proof with respect to his application for relief under
the CAT.
Preliminarily, I note that there is a dual system
for relief under the CAT.  The first form of relief under

102a

CAT is withholding of removal, which permits
withholding in a manner similar to the law under INA
section 241(b)(3).  8 C.F.R. § 1208.16©.  However,
there are several grounds for mandatory denial of
withholding of removal under the CAT, including
conviction for a particularly serious crime.  8 C.F.R.
§ 1208.16(d)(2).  The second form of relief under CAT,
deferral of removal, remains available to applicants
who are barred from withholding.  8 C.F.R. § 1208.17;
see Matter of Jean, 23 I. & N. Dec. 373, 376 n.7 (A.G.
2002) (asserting, “an alien’s criminal history is
irrelevant in examining his or her entitlement to
deferral of removal”).  Notably, however, an applicant
granted deferral of removal is subject to streamlined
termination where DHS has evidence undermining
the likelihood that the applicant would be subject to
torture in the country of removal.  8 C.F.R.
§ 1208.17(d).  Here, because Respondent’s conviction
under NYPL section 120.50(3) was found to  be for a
particularly serious crime, the only remaining form of
relief available to him under the CAT is deferral of
removal.  See Part IV(B)(ii) supra.
The regulations require that, in assessing whether
Respondent proved that he would more likely than
not be tortured in Egypt, I consider all evidence
relevant to the possibility of future torture.  8 C.F.R,
§ 1208.16(c)(3).  Relevant evidence includes, but is not
limited to: (1) evidence that Respondent suffered past
torture; (2) evidence that Respondent could relocate
to the another part of Egypt where he is not likely to
be tortured; (3) evidence of gross, flagrant or mass
violations of human rights; and (4) any other relevant
information regarding country conditions.  Id. at (i)–
(iv).  First, while I previo usly granted Respondent’s
application for asylum, the harm he suffered—being

103a

accosted and threatened by Muslims on account of his
Coptic Christian religion—is not severe enough to rise
to the level of torture.  8 C.F.R. § 1208.18(a)(1)
(“Torture is defined as any act by which severe pain
or suffering, whether physical or mental, is
intentionally inflicted on a person”).  Moreover, even
if the past harm Respondent suffered were
sufficiently severe, he failed to demonstrate that it
was inflicted by, at the instigation of, or with the
consent or acquiescence of a public official.  Id.  As to
the second factor, however, I recognize that
Respondent claims he would be targeted by Egyptian
police.  8 C.F.R.  § 1208.16(3)(ii).  Third, as Dr.
Marshall pointed out, the evidence on background
country conditions is consistent in describing the use
of torture in Egyptian prisons to be pervasive.  [Ex. 4,
at 4; Ex. R5, at 8, ¶ 31.1; Ex. 10, Attach. A, at 8,
¶ 31.1; Ex R11, Attach. B, at  5, ¶ 26; Ex. R13, at 8,
¶ 31; Ex. R14, at 6.]  Fo urth, I accept Dr. Marshall’s
testimony that Respondent could be convicted under
Egyptian Law 80(d), and that if he were imprisoned
he might suffer more harassment than other
prisoners guards because he is a Copt and because
would be considered an ally of the enemy Christian
West.
Nevertheless, the fact that  torture is systemic in
Egyptian prisons, and that Copts and those perceived
to be allied with the enemy Christian West might be
more attractive targets for such torture, does not
establish that Respondent would more likely than not
be tortured in Egypt.  See Matter of J–E–, 23 I. & N.
Dec. 291, 303 (BIA 2002) (sta nding alone, even a
pattern of gross, flagrant or mass violations of human
rights does not suffice to show that an applicant
would more likely than not be tortured in the country

104a

of removal).  Instead, Respondent must show that he
will personally be at risk of torture in the country of
removal.  Id.  However, I find that the evidence
regarding whether Respondent personally would
more likely than not be tortured in Egypt to be
tenuous, as Respondent seeks to carry his burden by
stringing together a series of suppositions.
As explained in Matter of J–F–F–, 23 I. & N. Dec.
912, 917–18 (A.G. 2006), a CAT applicant cannot cany
his burden by “stringing together a series of
suppositions.”  Instead, the CAT applicant he must
show “that each step in the hypothetical chain of
events is more likely than not to happen.”  Matter of
J–F–F–, 23 I. & N. Dec.  at 917–18.  Here, for
Respondent to prove he will more likely than not be
tortured he must prove all of the following: he will
more likely than not be discovered by Egyptian
officials; Egyptian officials will more likely than not
find out that he sought asylum, resided in, and was
convicted for a serious offense in the United States;
based on their knowledge of Respondent’s background
and interactions with the United States, Egyptian
officials will more likely than not charge and imprison
Respondent under Egyptian Law section 80(d); and
upon imprisonment, Egyptian officials will more
likely than not torture Respondent because he is a
Copt.
In examining the record for evidence, I recognize
that Dr. Marshall testified that Respondent could be
convicted for under Egyptian Law section 80(d),
because by applying for asylum and by being
convicted for a serious offense in the United States,
he maybe found to have damaged Egypt’s reputation.
Dr. Marshall’s testimony is insufficient for
Respondent to carry his burd en of proof, as he must

105a

prove that the preceding steps in his hypothetical
chain of events are more likely than not to occur.  See
Matter of J–F–F–, 23 I. & N. Dec. at 917–18.  Yet,
Respondent failed to prove the initial steps of his
hypothetical chain—that is, that he will more likely
than not be discovered by Egyptian police or that
upon discovering him that they will more likely than
not find out about his interactions with the United
States government.  In fact, Dr. Marshall testified
that he does not know how the Egyptian government
learns of its citizens’ criminal convictions and asylum
claims abroad.  While Dr. Marshall believes the
government might elicit such information from its
citizens when questioning them upon their return to
Egypt, he testified that, if a returnee denies being
convicted or having made asylum applications
abroad, he is not sure how the government would
learn of it.
Dr. Marshall testified that he knows of a case in
which an Egyptian man who applied for asylum in
Canada, when returned to Egypt, was detained.  Yet,
a single incident of detention and harm is far from
sufficient to establish the Egyptian government
routinely discovers, detains, and tortures returnees.
Therefore, this single ca se fails to prove that
Respondent would more likely than not be detained
upon his return to Egypt, or that upon his detention,
he would more likely that not be tortured.
Moreover, I find Khouzham v, Ashcroft, 361, F.3d
161 (2d Cir. 2004), where the Second Circuit granted
an applicant’s petition for review of the denial from
CAT deferral, distinguishable.  In Khouzham, the
Second Circuit was concerned that the petitioner
would more likely than not be discovered by the
Egyptian police, and thus be detained and tortured,

106a

because there were “serious reasons to believe” he had
committed, and was wanted for murder.  Id. at 166,
170–71.  By contrast, here the record lacks any
evidence that the Egyptian government is specifically
looking for the Respondent.  While there is evidence
that certain private individuals previously harmed
Respondent, neither Respondent nor Dr. Marshall
offered any evidence that the Egyptian government
might know of or punish Respondent for those
problems.  In fact, Respondent testified that he never
informed the police of his problems.  Therefore, unlike
in Khouzham, the record does not establish it is more
likely than not that upon his return, the Egyptian
government will capture, detain, or torture him.
Lastly, Dr. Marshall testified that Christians and
those viewed as allied with the Christian West are
often subject to disparate treatment, persecution, and
if in a detained setting, might be targeted for
proportionally more torture than other prisoners.
Nonetheless, evidence of disparate treatment or
persecution are insufficient to prove Respondent
would more likely than not be tortured in Egypt.
Moreover, even assuming it is true that if jailed.
Respondent would face a greater likelihood of torture
than other prisoners due to his religion and his
fifteen-year residency in the United States, the record
lacks sufficient evidence th at he would more likely
than not be imprisoned.  Furthermore, while Dr.
Marshall’s reports explain that the Egyptian
Constitution forbids Christians from witnessing,
evangelizing, or proselytizing, and that Christians
have been arrested for wi tnessing, Respondent has
not offered any evidence to establish he ever engaged
in such behavior, or that he would if returned to
Egypt.  [Ex. R5, at 6, ¶ 22 R10, at 6, ¶ 22; Ex. R13, at

107a

6, ¶ 22.]  Thus, Respondent has failed to prove that he
would more likely than not be tortured based on his
religion or perceived association with the Christian
West.
Based on the foregoing, I find that Respondent has
failed to carry his burden of proof to establish that he
would more likely than not be tortured if returned to
Egypt.
V.  Conclusion
Accordingly, after a careful review of the
record, the following order shall be entered:

The Department of Homeland Security initiated
removal proceedings against the respondent by filing
a Notice to Appear initially  back in March of 2019.

The respondent filed an I-589 on April 22, 2020.
The respondent has numerous convictions that are
particularly serious crimes.  Therefore, his form of
relief being sought is limited to deferral of removal
under the Convention against Torture.  The
respondent had initially entered the United States in
1995 and had received asylee status back in 1996.
After a series of convictions, the respondent’s asylee
status was terminated, and his application for
adjustment of status and wavier under 209 were
pretermitted, hence, the filing of the I-589 on April 22,
2020.
The respondent testified that his father was part
of the military commission in Guatemala back in
1995, and that as part of the military commission he
was involved in recruitment of soldiers and movement
of arms and ammunition.  The respondent testified
that a group of guerillas approached the respondent
in 1995 and asked him to join them, and that they
wanted information regarding things that the
respondent’s father may know, and if he joined them
that he would reap great benefits, money, houses,
whatever.  The respondent te stified that he said he
did not want to join them, and they said, well, you
need to think about it.
The respondent then was approached again by this
group of guerillas asking the same thing, and the
respondent, again, declined.  The respondent testified
that at that time, they kidnapped him and took him
to a place far away and ke pt him for approximately
three hours.  During that time, they beat him, and, at

130a

when he was released, th ey dumped him and in an
unknown place, and he we nt to a place near the
border, that the bleeding stopped and his face healed.
The respondent testified that he told his father
about the first time he was approached by the
guerillas, but he did not tell his father about the
second time that he was approached and kidnapped,
that he simply fled the country.
The respondent testified that the reason his
original I-589 filed back in 1996 is different in that
the original I-589 said that  he refused to join the
guerillas because of his religion and does not mention
his father is because someone else who helped him fill
this out told the respondent that the fact that he was
injured would be sufficient without all the extra
detail.  The respondent was asked about his religion
claim, and the respondent stated that, yes, one of the
reasons he did not want to join the guerillas is
because he believed in God and did not want to hurt
anyone else.  The respondent testified that he is afraid
to return to Guatemala because the same people that
used to part of the guerillas are now part of the cartel
and would recognize him and still come after him.
The Court finds that the discrepancies in the
respondent’s answers are not fatal to his asylum

An applicant for deferral of removal under the
Convention against Tortur e bears the burden of
proving that it is more likely than not that he would
be tortured if removed to the proposed country of

131a

removal.  Torture is defined as the intentional
infliction of severe physical or mental pain or
suffering based on discrimination of any kind, or for
the purpose of obtaining information or a confession,
or to punish for an act or suspected act, or to
intimidate or coerce any person or third party.  There
is also a requirement to show that a government actor
must consent or acquiesce or instigate the torture or
breach his or her legal responsibility to intervene to
prevent such torture because they are unwilling or
unable to oppose it if inflicted by a third party.
In assessing whether it is more likely than not that
the applicant will be tortured in the proposed country
of removal, the Court may consider evidence of past
torture, evidence the applicant could relocate to a part
of the party of removal where he is not likely to be
tortured, evidence of gr oss, flagrant or mass
violations of human rights within the country of
removal, or other relevant information.  An applicant
cannot string together a series of suppositions, and
the applicant must show sp ecific grounds indicating
that he would be personally at risk.
In the instant case, the respondent’s application
does not meet the burden for deferral of removal
under the Convention against Torture.  First of all,
the original asylum grant was just that, an asylum
grant.  The burden of proof is much lower than in a
CAT claim.  Therefore, the Court cannot rely on a
previous grant.
Also, the Court finds that while it does not condone
the actions of the guerillas, the respondent’s past
harm does not rise to the level of torture.  Having a
wound from being harmed does not automatically
mean torture.  The respondent did not need medical
care or chose not to get it, and stated himself that the

132a

wound healed itself.  While it does not make sense to
this Court why the respondent did not go to his father
after being attacked, even considering the
respondent’s credible testimony, there has not been
torture in the past.  The government in Guatemala
has changed and has made several changes in light of
the end of the civil war.  Several of the former
intelligence chiefs and people in the public ministry
that were involved in indigenous conflicts in the civil
war have had charges placed against them, and the
government appears to be working to rid itself of the
corruption not only that has lasted from the civil war
but also that just on a gene ral level such as on July
16 the public ministry brought charges against more
than 50 persons including 10 members of congress for
receiving kick-backs from construction and medical
supply procurement and for awarding public jobs by
irregular means.
As the Department mentioned, in 1996 the Peace
Accords were signed.  And as in Matter of A-B- and
Matter of M-E-V-G- and Matter of S-E-G-, the fear of
the cartel is not sufficient to meet the respondent’s
burden.  The government definitely is struggling with
issues within its country, but as Matter of J-F-F-
notes a lack of resources is regrettable, but it does not
constitute torture under the regulations.
The respondent states that he has heard that
there are many problems in his hometown.  At the
same time, the respondent states he does not have a
home anywhere in Guatemala.  Therefore, there is
nothing to show that the respondent cannot relocate
if he has issues in his hometown.  There is nothing in
the record to show that the government would either
consent to or look the other way if someone tried to
torture the respondent.

133a

In regards to the respondent’s claim that he would
be targeted because he has been diagnosed with
COVID-19 positive, the government does not consent
to treatment that COVID-p ositive deportees have
received and, in fact, as the Department noted in the
article under Exhibit 25, Tab H, talks about how the
government is working for ways to make sure that the
deportees are welcome back in without discrimination
and local community leaders are also doing the same.
Therefore, there is nothing in the record to support
that the respondent would be singled out, would be
tortured, and that the government would permit it
based on the respondent’s COVID-19 positive status.
Therefore, based on the fact that the respondent
has not suffered past torture, that the country
conditions have dramatically changed, that a fear of
cartel is not sufficient in light of Guatemala’s efforts
to control the cartels and discrimination and
corruption, and that the government has not shown
acquiescence and is not turning a blind eye to local
communities’ reactions to COVID-positive returnees,
the respondent has not met his burden to show that
he warrants a grant of deferral under the Convention
against Torture.
Therefore, it is hereby ordered that the
respondent’s application for asylum is denied.  The
respondent’s application for withholding of removal is
denied.  The respondent’s application for withholding
of removal under the Convention against Torture is
denied, and the respondent’s application for deferral
of removal under the Convention against Torture is
denied.  And the respondent is ordered removed to
Guatemala.

237(a)(1)(B) of the Immigration and
Nationality Act (“INA”), as contained in the
Notice to Appear (“NTA”).  Ex. 1.  The Court

under INA §208.
3.   That USCIS issued a Notice of Intent to
Terminate Asylum to respondent on February
13, 2019, because of respondent’s criminal
convictions.
4.  That the Court terminated respondent’s asylee
status as of July 1, 2019.
5.  That the Court denied respondent’s motion to
reconsider the termination of his asylee status
on August 20, 2019.
6.  That respondent has filed motions to continue
his individual hearing to request relief under
INA §209 and adjust hi s status to Lawful
Permanent Resident.
7.  That DHS opposes the motion to continue the
hearing and submitted a Motion to Pretermit
respondent’s adjustment of status application.

137a

I. Analysis
INA §209 governs the adjustment of status for
refugees and asylees.  INA §209 corresponds to 8 CFR
§1209.1 and 8 CFR §1209.2.  Since respondent was
admitted as an asylee, the Court will focus on 8 CFR
§1209.2, Adjustment of Status of Alien Granted
Asylum.  Subsection (a)(1 ) of 8 CFR §1209.2 states
“[e]xcept as provided in paragraph (a)(2) or (a)(3) of
this section, the status of any alien who has been
granted asylum in the United States may be adjusted
to that of an alien lawf ully admitted for permanent
resident…”
Subsection (2) of 8 CFR §1209.2 states “[a]n alien,
who was granted asylum in the United States prior to
November 29, 1990 (regardless of whether or not such
asylum has been terminated under section 208(b) of
the Act), and is no longer a refuges due a changed in
circumstances in the foreign state where he or she
feared persecution, may also have his or her status
adjusted by the director to that of an alien lawfully
admitted for permanent residence even if he or she is
no longer able to demonstrate that he or she continue
to be a refugee within the meaning of section
101(a)(42) of the Act…”
Lastly, subsection (3)(b) of 8 CFR §1209.2 states
“...[a]n applicant who is inadmissible to the United
States under section 212(a) of the Act, may, under
section 209(c) of the Act, have the grounds of
admissibility waived by the director...for
humanitarian purposes, to assure family unity, or
when it is otherwise in the public interest.
Respondent relies on Siwe v. Holder, 742 F.3d 603
(5th Cir. 2014) to bolster his claim that he is entitled
to apply for adjustment of status as a person “who has

138a

been granted asylum in the United States.”  In Siwe,
the 5th Circuit opined that the phrase “who has been
granted asylum” is to be read as anyone who has been
granted asylum in the past including those who have
had their status terminated.  The Court in Siwe looks
at the caveat carved out by 8 CFR §1209(2) and states
since Congress did not carve out an exception for
terminated asylees, they must mean anyone who has
ever been granted.  However, a reading of the Agency
notes on the Final Rule found in 57 FR 42883-01, 1992
W L  2 2 5 6 1 1 ( F . R . )  u n d e r c u t s  t h i s  f i n d i n g .   T h e  1 9 9 2
Final Rule adjusts the resident status allowed each
year under 209(b) of the INA from 5000 to 10000
adjustments.  Most importantly the Final Rule states
“[t]he law also provides for the adjustment of certain
aliens who have been granted asylum but who county
conditions changed so that they no longer continue to
be refugees within the definition of section 101(a)(42)
of the Immigration and Nationality Act.  This
provision applies to asylees who were or would be
qualified for adjustment as of November 28, 1990…”
Prior to this change, a refugee or asylee who could lose
their status solely due to a change in their country
conditions.  In other words, the caveat concerning
“whether or not such asylum has been terminated”
was to address a portion of the population that were
left in a legal gray area if there were changed country
conditions.  This caveat was not designed to say all
other refugees and asylee that have ever been granted
status can apply for adjustment notwithstanding the
current status they hold.  A person who has been
granted status, on its face, is a person who has been
granted status.  Full stop.  There is no reasonable
reading that would include adding something along

139a

the lines of notwithstanding the termination of their
status.
In Siwe, the Court also stated that reading the
statute any way other than through its analysis
would nullify the waiver available in 8 CFR §1209(b).
This line of reasoning misses the full breadth of the
waiver statute.  A person  can be granted asylee or
refugee status and yet, when it comes time for the
person to adjust, the person may be inadmissible for
a number of reasons that do  not include termination
of their asylum status.  The grounds of inadmissibility
for a grant of asylee or refugee status are extremely
narrow compared to the grounds of inadmissibility for
a grant of adjustment of status.  A person who has
been admitted as an asylee and remains an asylee can
apply for adjustment of status and still need a waiver.
The Court in Siwe made a leap in reasoning that
excluded the myriad of possibilities still viable under
INA §209(c) waiver.  It is also noteworthy that the
Board of Immigration Appeals have held that the
termination of asylee status bars adjustment under
INA §209 and that no other Circuit has adopted the
reasoning in Siwe.
Accordingly, after a careful review of the record,
the following Orders will be entered:
